A core file or <e0>core dump</e0> is sometimes generated when things go wrong with a program during its execution. The core file contains a copy of the system's memory, as it was at the time that the error occured.

Compressed files are useful because they take less space on your hard disk. Another advantage is that it takes less bandwidth to send a compressed file over your network. A lot of files, such as the man pages, are stored in a compressed format on your system. Yet unpacking these to get a little bit of information and then having to compress them again is rather time-consuming. You don't want to unpack a man page, for instance, read about an option to a command and then compress the man page again. Most people will probably forget to clean up after they found the information they needed.

So we have tools that work on compressed files, by uncompressing them only in memory. The actual compressed file stays on your disk as it is. Most systems support <c0>zgrep</c0>, <c1>zcat</c1>, <c2>bzless</c2> and other members of the z-family to prevent unnecessary decompressing/compressing actions. See your system's binary directory and the Info pages.
See <x0/> for more on the actual compressing of files and examples on making archives.

We already mentioned a couple of environment variables, such as <v0>PATH</v0> and <v1>HOME</v1>. Until now, we only saw examples in which they serve a certain purpose to the shell. But there are many other Linux utilities that need information about you in order to do a good job.
What other information do programs need apart from paths and home directories?

A lot of programs want to know about the kind of terminal you are using; this information is stored in the <v0>TERM<i1/></v0> variable. In text mode, this will be the <e2>linux</e2> terminal emulation, in graphical mode you are likely to use <e3>xterm</e3>. Lots of programs want to know what your favorite editor is, in case they have to start an editor in a subprocess. The shell you are using is stored in the <v4>SHELL<i5/></v4> variable, the operating system type in <v6>OS<i7/></v6> and so on. A list of all variables currently defined for your session can be viewed<i8/> entering the <c9>printenv<i10/></c9> command.

The environment variables are managed by the shell. As opposed to regular shell variables, environment variables are inherited by any program you start, including another shell. New processes are assigned a copy of these variables, which they can read, modify and pass on in turn to their own child processes.

There is nothing special about variable names, except that the common ones are in upper case characters by convention. You may come up with any name you want, although there are standard variables that are important enough to be the same on every Linux system, such as <v0>PATH</v0> and <v1>HOME</v1>.

A lot of variables are not only predefined but also preset, using configuration files. We discuss these in the next section.

When entering the <c0>ls <o1>-al</o1></c0> command to get a long listing of all files, including the ones starting with a dot, in your home directory, you will see one or more files starting with a . and ending in <e2>rc</e2>. For the case of <c3>bash</c3>, this is <f4>.bashrc<i5/></f4>. This is the counterpart of the system-wide configuration file <f6>/etc/bashrc<i7/></f6>.

When logging<i0/> into an interactive login shell, <c1>login</c1> will do the authentication, set the environment and start your shell. In the case of <c2>bash</c2>, the next step is reading the general <f3>profile<i4/></f3> from <f5>/etc</f5>, if that file exists. <c6>bash</c6> then looks for <f7>~/.bash_profile<i8/></f7>, <f9>~/.bash_login<i10/></f9> and <f11>~/.profile<i12/></f11>, in that order, and reads and executes commands from the first one that exists and is readable. If none exists, <f13>/etc/bashrc</f13> is applied.
When a login shell exits, <c0>bash</c0> reads and executes commands from the file <f1>~/.bash_logout<i2/></f1>, if it exists.
This procedure is explained in detail in the <c0>login<i1/></c0> and <c2>bash</c2> man pages.
A typical set of setup files
Let's look<i0/> at some of these config files. First <f1>/etc/profile</f1> is read, in which important variables such as <v2>PATH</v2>, <v3>USER</v3> and <v4>HOSTNAME</v4> are set:

<p0>debby:~></p0> <c1>cat /etc/profile</c1>
# /etc/profile

# System wide environment and startup programs, for login setup
# Functions and aliases go in /etc/bashrc


# Path manipulation
if [ `id -u` = 0 ] && ! echo $PATH | /bin/grep -q "/sbin" ; then
    PATH=/sbin:$PATH
fi

if [ `id -u` = 0 ] && ! echo $PATH | /bin/grep -q "/usr/sbin" ; then
    PATH=/usr/sbin:$PATH
fi

if [ `id -u` = 0 ] && ! echo $PATH | /bin/grep -q "/usr/local/sbin"
    then
    PATH=/usr/local/sbin:$PATH
fi

if ! echo $PATH | /bin/grep -q "/usr/X11R6/bin" ; then
    PATH="$PATH:/usr/X11R6/bin"
fi

These lines check the path to set: if <e0>root</e0> opens a shell (user ID 0), it is checked that <f1>/sbin</f1>, <f2>/usr/sbin</f2> and <f3>/usr/local/sbin</f3> are in the path. If not, they are added. It is checked for everyone that <f4>/usr/X11R6/bin</f4> is in the path.

# No core files by default
ulimit -S -c 0 > /dev/null 2>&1
All trash goes to <f0>/dev/null</f0> if the user doesn't change this setting.
Here general variables are assigned their proper values.

export PATH USER LOGNAME MAIL HOSTNAME HISTSIZE INPUTRC
All variables are exported, so that they are available to other programs requesting information about your environment.

for i in /etc/profile.d/*.sh ; do
    if [ -r $i ]; then
    	. $i
    fi
done

All readable shell scripts from the <f0>/etc/profile.d<i1/></f0> directory are read and executed. These do things like enabling <e2>color-ls</e2>, aliasing <c3>vi</c3> to <c4>vim</c4>, setting locales etc. The temporary variable <v5>i</v5> is unset to prevent it from disturbing shell behavior later on.
Then <c0>bash</c0> looks for a <f1>.bash_profile</f1> in the user's home<i2/> directory:

This very straight forward file instructs your shell to first read <f0>~/.bashrc</f0> and then <f1>~/.bash_login</f1>. You will encounter the <c2>source<i3/></c2> built-in shell command regularly when working in a shell environment: it is used to apply configuration changes to the current environment.

The <f0>~/.bash_login</f0> file<i1/> defines default file protection by setting the <c2>umask</c2> value, see <x3/>. The <f4>~/.bashrc</f4> file is used to define a bunch of user-specific aliases and functions and personal environment variables. It first reads <f5>/etc/bashrc</f5>, which describes the default prompt (<v6>PS1</v6>) and the default umask value. After that, you can add your own settings. If no <f7>~/.bashrc</f7> exists, <f8>/etc/bashrc</f8> is read by default.
Your <f0>/etc/bashrc</f0> file<i1/> might look like this:

<p0>debby:~></p0> <c1>cat /etc/bashrc</c1>
# /etc/bashrc

# System wide functions and aliases
# Environment stuff goes in /etc/profile

# by default, we want this to get set.
# Even for non-interactive, non-login shells.
if [ `id -gn` = `id -un` -a `id -u` -gt 99 ]; then
	umask 002
else
	umask 022
fi
These lines set the <c0>umask</c0> value. Then, depending on the type of shell, the prompt is set:

	xterm*)

	else
   PROMPT_COMMAND='echo -ne "\033]0;${USER}@${HOSTNAME%%.*}:\
${PWD/$HOME/~}\007"'
	fi
    ;;
	*)

/etc/sysconfig/bash-prompt-default
	    ;;
    esac

Upon logout, the commands in <f0>~/.bash_logout</f0> are<i1/> executed, which can for instance clear the terminal, so that you have a clean window upon logging out of a remote session, or upon leaving the system console:
Let's take a closer look at how these scripts work in the next section. Keep <c0>info <p1>bash</p1></c0> close at hand.

The <a0>Bash</a0> prompt can do much more than displaying such simple information as your user name, the name of your machine and some indication about the present working directory. We can add other information such as the current date and time, number of connected users etc.
Before we begin, however, we will save our current prompt<i0/> in another environment variable:

When we change<i0/> the prompt now, for example by issuing the command <c1><v2>PS1</v2>=<r3>"->"</r3></c1>, we can always get our original prompt back with the command <c4><v5>PS1</v5>=<v6>$MYPROMPT</v6></c4>. You will, of course, also get it back when you reconnect, as long as you just fiddle with the prompt on the command line and avoid putting it in a shell configuration file.
In order to understand these prompts<i0/> and the escape sequences used, we refer to the <a1>Bash Info</a1> or man pages.

Variables are exported so the subsequently executed commands will also know about the environment. The prompt configuration line that you want is best put in your shell configuration file, <f0>~/.bashrc<i1/></f0>.

If you want, prompts can execute shell scripts and behave different under different conditions. You can even have the prompt play a tune every time you issue a command, although this gets boring pretty soon. More information can be found in the <u0>Bash-Prompt HOWTO</u0>.

A shell<i0/> script is, as we saw in the shell configuration examples, a text file containing shell commands. When such a file is used as the first non-option argument when invoking <a1>Bash</a1>, and neither the <o2>-c</o2> nor <o3>-s</o3> option is supplied, <a4>Bash</a4> reads and executes commands from the file, then exits. This mode of operation creates a non-interactive shell. When <a5>Bash</a5> runs a shell script, it sets the special parameter <v6>0</v6> to the name of the file, rather than the name of the shell, and the positional parameters (everything following the name of the script) are set to the remaining arguments, if any are given. If no additional arguments are supplied, the positional parameters are unset.

A shell script may be made executable by using the <c0>chmod<i1/></c0> command to turn on the execute bit. When <a2>Bash</a2> finds such a file while searching the <v3>PATH</v3> for a command, it spawns a sub-shell to execute it. In other words, executing

if <q0>filename</q0> is an executable shell script. This sub-shell reinitializes itself, so that the effect is as if a new shell had been invoked to interpret the script, with the exception that the locations of commands remembered by the parent (see <c1>hash</c1> in the <a2>Info</a2> pages) are retained by the child.

Most versions of UNIX make this a part of the operating system's command execution mechanism. If the first line of a script begins with the two characters <q0>#!</q0>, the remainder of the line specifies an interpreter for the program. Thus, you can specify <c1>bash</c1>, <c2>awk</c2>, <c3>perl</c3> or some other interpreter or shell and write the rest of the script file in that language.

The arguments to the interpreter consist of a single optional argument following the interpreter name on the first line of the script file, followed by the name of the script file, followed by the rest of the arguments. <a0>Bash</a0> will perform this action on operating systems that do not handle it themselves.

Here is a script consisting of some more lines, that I use to make backup copies of all files in a directory. The script first makes a list of all the files in the current directory and puts it in the variable <v0>LIST</v0>. Then it sets the name of the copy for each file, and then it copies the file. For each file, a message is printed:

<p0>tille:~></p0> <c1>cat <f2>bin/makebackupfiles.sh</f2></c1>
#!/bin/bash
# make copies of all files in a directory
LIST=`ls`
for i in $LIST; do
	ORIG=$i
	DEST=$i.old
	cp $ORIG $DEST
	echo "copied $i"
done

Just entering a line like <c0>mv <p1>*</p1> <p2>*.old</p2></c0> won't work, as you will notice when trying this on a set of test files. An <c3>echo</c3> command was added in order to display some activity. <c4>echo</c4>'s are generally useful when a script won't work: insert one after each doubted step and you will find the error in no time.
The <f0>/etc/rc.d/init.d</f0> directory contains loads of examples. Let's look at this script that controls<i1/> the fictive ICanSeeYou server:

#!/bin/sh
# description: ICanSeeYou allows you to see networked people

# process name: ICanSeeYou
# pidfile: /var/run/ICanSeeYou/ICanSeeYou.pid
# config: /etc/ICanSeeYou.cfg

# Source function library.
. /etc/rc.d/init.d/functions

# See how (with which arguments) we were called.
case "$1" in
	start)
		echo -n "Starting ICanSeeYou: "
		daemon ICanSeeYou
		echo
		touch /var/lock/subsys/ICanSeeYou
		;;
	stop)
		echo -n "Shutting down ICanSeeYou: "
		killproc ICanSeeYou
		echo
		rm -f /var/lock/subsys/ICanSeeYou
		rm -f /var/run/ICanSeeYou/ICanSeeYou.pid
		;;
	status)
		status ICanSeeYou
		;;
	restart)
		$0 stop
		$0 start
		;;
	*)
		echo "Usage: $0 {start|stop|restart|status}"
		exit 1
esac

exit 0

First, with the <c0>.</c0> command (dot) a set of shell functions, used by almost all shell scripts in <f1>/etc/rc.d/init.d</f1>, is loaded. Then a <c2>case</c2> command is issued, which defines 4 different ways the script can execute. An example might be <c3>ICanSeeYou <p4>start</p4></c3>. The decision of which case to apply is made by reading the (first) argument to the script, with the expression <e5>$1</e5>.

When no compliant input is given, the default case, marked with an asterisk, is applied, upon which the script gives an error message. The <c0>case</c0> list is ended with the <c1>esac</c1> statement. In the <e2>start</e2> case the server program is started as a daemon, and a process ID and lock are assigned. In the <e3>stop</e3> case, the server process is traced down and stopped, and the lock and the PID are removed. Options, such as the <o4>daemon</o4> option, and functions like <o5>killproc</o5>, are defined in the <f6>/etc/rc.d/init.d/functions</f6> file. This setup is specific to the distribution used in this example. The initscripts on your system might use other functions, defined in other files, or none at all.
Upon success, the script returns an exit code of zero to its parent.

This script is a fine example of using functions, which make the script easier to read and the work done faster. Note that they use <c0>sh</c0> instead of <c1>bash</c1>, to make them useful on a wider range of systems. On a Linux system, calling <c2>bash</c2> as <c3>sh</c3> results in the shell running in POSIX-compliant mode.

The <c0>bash</c0> man pages contain more information about combining commands, <c1>for</c1>- and <c2>while</c2>-loops and regular expressions, as well as examples. A comprehensible <a3>Bash</a3> course for system administrators and power users, with exercises, from the same author as this Introduction to Linux guide, is at <u4>http://tille.garrels.be/training/bash/</u4>. Detailed description of <a5>Bash</a5> features and applications is in the reference guide <u6>Advanced Bash Scripting</u6>.

The average user may not care too much about his login settings, but Linux offers a wide variety of flashy window and desktop managers for use under X, the graphical<i0/> environment. The use and configuration of window managers and desktops is straightforward and may even resemble the standard MS Windows, Apple or UNIX CDE environment, although many Linux users prefer flashier desktops and fancier window managers. We won't discuss the user specific configuration here. Just experiment and read the documentation using the built-in Help functions these managers provide and you will get along fine.
We will, however, take a closer look at the underlying system.

The X Window<i0/> System is a network-transparent window system which runs on a wide range of computing and graphics machines. X Window System servers run on computers with bitmap displays. The X server distributes user input to and accepts output requests from several client<i1/> programs through a variety of different interprocess communication channels. Although the most common case is for the client programs to be running on the same machine as the server, clients can be run transparently from other machines (including machines with different architectures and operating systems) as well. We will learn how to do this in <x2/> on networking and remote applications.

X supports overlapping hierarchical sub-windows and text and graphics operations, on both monochrome and color displays. The number of X client programs that use the X server is quite large. Some of the programs provided in the core X Consortium<i0/> distribution include:
<c0>xset</c0>, <c1>xmodmap</c1> and many others: user preference setting programs
<c0>xlsfonts</c0> and others: a font displayer, utilities for listing information about fonts, windows and displays

We refer again to the man pages of these commands for detailed information. More explanations on available functions can be found in the <e0>Xlib - C language X Interface</e0> manual that comes with your X distribution, the <e1>X Window System Protocol</e1> specification, and the various manuals and documentation of X toolkits. The <f2>/usr/share/doc</f2> directory contains references to these documents and many others.

Many other utilities, window managers, games, toolkits and gadgets are included as user-contributed software in the X Consortium distribution, or are available using anonymous FTP on the Internet. Good places to start are <u0>http://www.x.org</u0> and <u1>http://www.xfree.org</u1>.

Furthermore, all your graphical applications, such as your browser, your E-mail program, your image viewing programs, sound playing tools and so on, are all clients to your X server. Note that in normal operation, that is in graphical mode, X clients and the X server on Linux run on the same machine.
From the user's perspective, every X server<i0/> has a <e1>display name</e1> in the form of:
This information is used by the application to determine how it should connect to the X server and which screen it should use by default (on displays with multiple monitors):

<e0>hostname<i1/></e0>: The host name specifies the name of the client machine to which the display is physically connected. If the host name is not given, the most efficient way of communicating to a server on the same machine will be used.

<e0>displaynumber<i1/></e0>: The phrase <q2>display</q2> is usually used to refer to a collection of monitors that share a common key board and pointer (mouse, tablet, etc.). Most workstations tend to only have one keyboard, and therefore, only one display. Larger, multi-user systems, however, frequently have several displays so that more than one person can be doing graphics work at once. To avoid confusion, each display on a machine is assigned a <e3>display number</e3> (beginning at 0) when the X server for that display is started. The display number must always be given in a display name.

<e0>screen number<i1/></e0>: Some displays share a single keyboard and pointer among two or more monitors. Since each monitor has its own set of windows, each screen is assigned a <e2>screen number</e2> (beginning at 0) when the X server for that display is started. If the screen number is not given, screen 0 will be used.

On POSIX systems, the default display name is stored in your <v0>DISPLAY<i1/></v0> environment variable. This variable is set automatically by the <c2>xterm</c2> terminal emulator. However, when you log into another machine on a network, you might need to set <v3>DISPLAY</v3> by hand to point to your display, see <x4/>.
More information can be found in the X man pages.

The layout of windows on the screen is controlled by special programs called <e0>window managers<i1/></e0>. Although many window managers will honor geometry specifications as given, others may choose to ignore them (requiring the user to explicitly draw the window's region on the screen with the pointer, for example).

Since window managers are regular (albeit complex) client programs, a variety of different user interfaces can be built. The X Consortium distribution comes with a window manager named <c0>twm</c0>, but most users prefer something more fancy when system resources permit. Sawfish and Enlightenment are popular examples which allow each user to have a desktop according to mood and style.

A desktop manager makes use of one window manager or another for arranging your graphical desktop in a convenient way, with menubars, drop-down menus, informative messages, a clock, a program manager, a file manager and so on. Among the most popular desktop managers are <a0>Gnome</a0> and <a1>KDE</a1>, which both run on almost any Linux distribution and many other UNIX systems.
KDE applications in Gnome/Gnome applications in KDE

You don't need to start your desktop in <a0>KDE</a0> in order to be able to run <a1>KDE</a1> applications. If you have the <a2>KDE</a2> libraries installed (the <a3>kdelibs</a3> package), you can run these applications from the <a4>Gnome</a4> menus or start them from a <a5>Gnome</a5> terminal.

Running <a0>Gnome</a0> applications in a <a1>KDE</a1> environment is a bit more tricky, because there is no single set of base-libraries in <a2>Gnome</a2>. However, the dependencies and thus extra packages you might have to install will become clear when running or installing such an application.

The X<i0/> distribution that used to come with Linux, <e1>XFree86</e1>, uses the configuration file <f2>XF86Config</f2> for its initial setup. This file configures your video card and is searched for in a number of locations, although it is usually in <f3>/etc/X11</f3>.
If you see that the file <f0>/etc/X11/XF86Config<i1/></f0> is present on your system, a full description can be found in the <a2>Info</a2> or man pages about <f3>XF86Config</f3>.

Because of licensing issues with XFree86, newer systems usually come with the <e0>X.Org<i1/></e0> distribution of the X server and tools. The main configuration file here is <f2>xorg.conf<i3/></f2>, usually also in <f4>/etc/X11</f4>. The file consists of a number of sections that may occur in any order. The sections contain information about your monitor, your video adaptor, the screen configuration, your keyboard etcetera. As a user, you needn't worry too much about what is in this file, since everything is normally determined at the time the system is installed.

Should you need to change graphical server settings, however, you can run the configuration tools or edit the configuration files that set up the infrastructure to use the XFree86 server. See the man pages for more information; your distribution might have its own tools. Since misconfiguration may result in unreadable garbage in graphical mode, you may want to make a backup copy of the configuration file before attempting to change it, just to be on the safe side.

Setting the <i0/>keyboard layout is done using the <c1>loadkeys<i2/></c1> command for text consoles. Use your local X configuration tool or edit the <e3>Keyboard</e3> section in <f4>XF86Config<i5/></f4> manually to configure the layout for graphical mode. The <v6>XkbdLayout<i7/></v6> is the one you want to set:

This is the default. Change it to your local settings by replacing the quoted value with any of the names listed in the subdirectories of your <f0>keymaps</f0> directory. If you can't find the keymaps, try displaying their location on your system issuing the command
It is possible to combine layout settings, like in this example:
Make a backup of the <f0>/etc/X11/XF86Config</f0> file before editing it! You will need to use the <e1>root</e1> account to do this.
Log out and reconnect in order to reload X settings.

The <a0>Gnome Keyboard Applet</a0> enables real-time switching<i1/> between layouts; no special pemissions are needed for using this program. <a2>KDE</a2> has a similar tool for switching between keyboard layouts.

Use<i0/> the <c1>setfont<i2/></c1> tool to load fonts in text mode. Most systems come with a standard <f3>inputrc<i4/></f3> file which enables combining of characters, such as the French <q5>é</q5> (meta characters). The system admin should then add the line

Setting time information<i0/> is usually done at installation time. After that, it can be kept up to date using an <e1>NTP<i2/></e1> (Network Time Protocol) client. Most Linux systems run <c3>ntpd</c3> by default:

You can run <c0>ntpdate<i1/></c0> manually to set the time, on condition that you can reach a time server. The <c2>ntpd</c2> daemon should not be running when you adjust the time using <c3>ntpdate</c3>. Use a time server as argument to the command:

<p0>root@box:~# </p0><c1>ntpdate <p2>10.2.5.200</p2></c1>
26 Oct 14:35:42 ntpdate[20364]: adjust time server 10.2.5.200 offset
 -0.008049 sec

See your system manual and the documentation that comes with the NTP package. Most desktop managers include tools to set the system time, providing that you have access to the system administrator's account.

For setting the time zone<i0/> correct, you can use <c1>tzconfig<i2/></c1> or <c3>timezone<i4/></c3> commands. Timezone information is usually set during the installation of your machine. Many systems have distribution-specific tools to configure it, see your system documentation.

If you'd rather get your messages<i0/> from the system in Dutch or French, you may want to set the <v1>LANG<i2/></v1> and <v3>LANGUAGE<i4/></v3> environment variables, thus enabling locale support for the desired language and eventually the fonts related to character conventions in that language.
With most graphical login<i0/> systems, such as <c1>gdm</c1> or <c2>kdm</c2>, you have the possibility to configure these language settings before logging in.

Note that on most systems, the default tends to be <e0>en_US.UTF-8<i1/></e0> these days. This is not a problem, because systems where this is the default, will also come with all the programs supporting this encoding. Thus, <c2>vi</c2> can edit all the files on your system, <c3>cat</c3> won't behave strange and so on.

Trouble starts when you connect to an older system not supporting this font encoding, or when you open a <e0>UTF-8<i1/></e0> encoded file on a system supporting only 1-byte character fonts. The <c2>recode<i3/></c2> utility might come in handy to convert files from one character set to another. Read the man pages for an overview of features and usage. Another solution might be to temporarily work with another encoding definition, by setting the <v4>LANG</v4> environment variable:

<p0>debby:~></p0> <c1>acroread /var/tmp/51434s.pdf</c1>
Warning: charset "UTF-8" not supported, using "ISO8859-1".
Aborted

<p2>debby:~></p2> <c3>set | grep UTF</c3>
LANG=en_US.UTF-8

<p4>debby:~></p4> <c5>export LANG=en_US</c5>

<p6>debby:~></p6> <c7>acroread /var/tmp/51434s.pdf</c7>
<--new window opens-->

Refer to the <u0>Mozilla</u0> web site for guidance on how to get <a1>Firefox</a1> in your language. The <u2>OpenOffice.org</u2> web site has information on localization of your <a3>OpenOffice.org</a3> suite.

The <u0>list of HOWTOs</u0> contains references to Bangla, Belarusian, Chinese, Esperanto, Finnish, Francophone, Hebrew, Hellenic, Latvian, Polish, Portugese, Serbian, Slovak, Slovenian, Spanish, Thai and Turkish localization instructions.

Most people are surprised to see that they have a running, usable computer after installing Linux; most distributions contain ample support for video and network cards, monitors and other external devices, so there is usually no need to install extra drivers. Also common tools such as office suites, web browsers, E-mail and other network client programs are included in the main distributions. Even so, an initial installation might not meet your requirements.

If you just can't find<i0/> what you need, maybe it is not installed on your system. It may also be that you have the required software, but it does not do what it is supposed to do. Remember that Linux moves fast, and software improves on a daily basis. Don't waste your time troubleshooting problems that might already be resolved.

You can update your system or add packages to it at any time you want. Most software comes in packages. Extra software may be found on your installation CDs or on the Internet. The website of your Linux distribution is a good place to start looking for additional software and contains instructions about how to install it on your type of Linux, see <x0/>. Always read the documentation that comes with new software, and any installation guidelines the package might contain. All software comes with a <f1>README<i2/></f1> file, which you are very strongly advised to read.

RPM, the <a0>RedHat Package Manager<i1/></a0>, is a powerful package manager that you can use to install, update and remove packages. It allows you to search for packages and keeps track of the files that come with each package. A system is built-in so that you can verify the authenticity of packages downloaded from the Internet. Advanced users can build their own packages with RPM.

An RPM package consists of an archive of files and meta-data used to install and erase the archive files. The meta-data includes helper scripts, file attributes, and descriptive information about the package. Packages come in two varieties: binary packages, used to encapsulate software to be installed, and source packages, containing the source code and recipe necessary to produce binary packages.

Many other distributions support RPM packages, among the popular ones RedHat Enterprise Linux, Mandriva (former Mandrake), Fedora Core and SuSE Linux. Apart from the advice for your distribution, you will want to read <c0>man <p1>rpm</p1></c0>.

Most packages are simply installed with the upgrade option, <o0>-U</o0>, whether the package is already installed or not. The RPM package contains a complete<i1/> version of the program, which overwrites existing versions or installs as a new package. The typical usage<i2/> is as follows:
The <o0>-v</o0> option generates more verbose output, and <o1>-h</o1> makes <c2>rpm</c2> print a progress bar:

New kernel packages, however, are installed with the install option <o0>-i</o0>, which does not overwrite existing version(s) of the package. That way, you will still be able to boot your system with the old kernel if the new one does not work.
You can also use <c0>rpm<i1/></c0> to check whether a package is installed<i2/> on your system:

<p0>[david@jupiter ~]</p0> <c1>rpm -qa | grep vim</c1>
vim-minimal-6.1-29
vim-X11-6.1-29
vim-enhanced-6.1-29
vim-common-6.1-29
Or you can find out which package contains a certain file<i0/> or executable:
Note that you need not have access to administrative privileges in order to use <c0>rpm</c0> to query the RPM database. You only need to be <e1>root</e1> when adding, modifying or deleting packages.
Below is one last example, demonstrating how to uninstall<i0/> a package using <c1>rpm</c1>:
Note that uninstalling is not that verbose by default, it is normal that you don't see much happening. When in doubt, use <c0>rpm <o1>-qa</o1></c0> again to verify that the package has been removed.
RPM can do much more than the couple of basic functions we discussed in this introduction; the <u0>RPM HOWTO</u0> contains further references.

This package format<i0/> is the default on Debian GNU/Linux, where <c1>dselect<i2/></c1>, and, nowadays more common, <c3>aptitude<i4/></c3>, is the standard tool for managing the packages. It is used to select packages that you want to install or upgrade, but it will also run during the installation of a Debian system and help you to define the access method to use, to list available packages and to configure packages.
The <u0>Debian web site</u0> contains all information you need, including a <q1>dselect Documentation for Beginners</q1>.

According to the latest news, the Debian package format is becoming more and more popular. At the time of this writing, 5 of the top-10 distributions use it. Also <c0>apt-get<i1/></c0> (see <x2/> is becoming extremely popular, also on non-DEB systems.
Checking whether a package is installed is done using the <c0>dpkg</c0> command. For instance, if you want to know which version of the <a1>Gallery</a1> software is installed on your machine:

<p0>nghtwsh@gorefest:~$ </p0><c1>dpkg <o2>-l</o2> <p3>*gallery*</p3></c1>
Desired=Unknown/Install/Remove/Purge/Hold
| Status=Not/Installed/Config-files/Unpacked/Failed-config/Half-installed
|/ Err?=(none)/Hold/Reinst-required/X=both-problems (Status,Err: uppercase=bad)
||/ Name           Version        Description
+++-==============-==============-============================================
ii  gallery        1.5-1sarge2    a web-based photo album written in php
The <q0>ii</q0> prefix means the package is installed. Should you see <q1>un</q1> as a prefix, that means that the package is known in the list that your computer keeps, but that it is not installed.
Searching which package a file belongs to is done using the <o0>-S</o0> to <c1>dpkg</c1>:
More information can be found in the <a0>Info</a0> pages for <c1>dpkg</c1>.

The largest part of Linux programs is Free/Open Source, so source<i0/> packages are available for these programs. Source files are needed for compiling your own program version. Sources for a program can be downloaded from its web site, often as a compressed tarball (<f1>program-version.tar.gz</f1> or similar). For RPM-based distributions, the source is often provided in the <f2>program-version.src.rpm</f2>. Debian, and most distributions based on it, provide themselves the adapted source which can be obtained using <c3>apt-get <p4>source</p4></c3>.

Specific requirements, dependencies and installation instructions are provided in the <f0>README</f0> file. You will probably need a C compiler, <c1>gcc</c1>. This GNU C compiler is included in most Linux systems and is ported to many other platforms.
The first thing you do after installing a new system is applying updates; this applies to all operating systems and Linux is not different.

The updates for most Linux<i0/> systems can usually be found on a nearby site mirroring your distribution. Lists of sites offering this service can be found at your distribution's web site, see <x1/>.

Updates<i0/> should be applied regularly, daily if possible - but every couple of weeks would be a reasonable start. You really should try to have the most recent version of your distribution, since Linux changes constantly. As we said before, new features, improvements and bug fixes are supplied at a steady rhythm, and sometimes important security problems are addressed.

The good news is that most Linux distributions provide tools so that you don't have to upgrade tens of packages daily by hand. The following sections give an overview of <e0>package manager managers.</e0> There is much more to this subject, even regular updates of source packages is manageable automatically; we only list the most commonly known systems. Always refer to the documentation for your specific distribution for advised procedures.

The <a0>Advanced Package Tool</a0> is a management<i1/> system for software packages. The command line tool for handling packages is <c2>apt-get<i3/></c2>, which comes with an excellent man page describing how to install and update packages and how to upgrade singular packages or your entire distribution. APT has its roots in the Debian GNU/Linux distribution, where it is the default manager for the Debian packages. APT has been ported to work with RPM packages as well. The main advantage of APT is that it is free and flexible to use. It will allow you to set up systems similar to the distribution specific (and in some cases commercial) ones listed in the next sections.
Generally, when first using<i0/> <c1>apt-get</c1>, you will need to get an index of the available packages. This is done using the command
After that<i0/>, you can use <c1>apt-get</c1> to upgrade your system:
Do this often, it's an easy way to keep your system up-to-date and thus safe.
Apart from this general usage, <c0>apt-get</c0> is also very fast for installing<i1/> individual packages. This is how it works:

<p0>[david@jupiter ~]</p0> <c1>su - -c "apt-get install xsnow"</c1>

Note the <o0>-c</o0> option to the <c1>su</c1> command, which indicates to the root shell to only execute this command, and then return to the user's environment. This way, you cannot forget to quit the root account.
If there are any dependencies on other packages, <c0>apt-get</c0> will download and install these supporting packages.
More information can be found in the <u0>APT HOWTO</u0>.

<a0>Update Agent<i1/></a0>, which originally only supported RedHat RPM packages, is now ported to a wider set of software, including non-RedHat repositories. This tool provides a complete system for updating the RPM packages on a RedHat or Fedora Core system. On the command line, type <c2>up2date<i3/></c2> to update your system. On the desktop, by default a small icon is activated, telleng you whether or not there are updates available for your system.

<a0>Yellowdog's Updater Modified<i1/></a0> (<c2>yum<i3/></c2>) is another tool that recently became more popular. It is an interactive but automated update program for installing, updating or removing RPM packages on a system. It is the tool of choice on Fedora systems.

On SuSE Linux, everything is done with <a0>YaST<i1/></a0>, Yet another Setup Tool, which supports a wide variety of system administration tasks, among which updating RPM packages. Starting from SuSE Linux 7.1 you can also upgrade using a web interface and <a2>YOU<i3/></a2>, Yast Online Update.

Mandrake Linux and Mandriva provide so-called URPMI<i0/> tools, a set of wrapper programs that make installing new software easier for the user. These tools combine with <a1>RPMDrake</a1> and <a2>MandrakeUpdate</a2> to provide everything needed for smooth install and uninstall of software packages. MandrakeOnline offers an extended range of services and can automatically notify administrators when updates are available for your particular Mandrake system. See <c3>man <p4>urpmi</p4></c3>, among others, for more info.
Also the <a0>KDE</a0> and <a1>Gnome</a1> desktop suites have their own (graphical) versions of package managers.

Most Linux installations are fine if you periodically upgrade your distribution. The upgrade<i0/> procedure will install a new kernel<i1/> when needed and make all necessary changes to your system. You should only compile or install a new kernel manually if you need kernel features that are not supported by the default kernel included in your Linux distribution.
Whether compiling your own optimized kernel or using a pre-compiled kernel package, install it in co-existence with the old kernel until you are sure that everything works according to plan.
Then create a dual boot system that will allow you to choose which kernel to boot by updating your boot loader configuration file <f0>grub.conf<i1/></f0>. This is a simple example:

# grub.conf generated by anaconda
#
# Note that you do not have to rerun grub after making config changes. 
# NOTICE:  You have a /boot partition.  This means that
#          all kernel and initrd paths are relative to /boot/, e.g.
#          root (hd0,0)
#          kernel /vmlinuz-version ro root=/dev/hde8
#          initrd /initrd-version.img
#boot=/dev/hde
default=0
timeout=10
splashimage=(hd0,0)/grub/splash.xpm.gz
title Red Hat Linux new (2.4.9-31)
	root (hd0,0)
	kernel /vmlinuz-2.4.9-31 ro root=/dev/hde8
	initrd /initrd-2.4.9-31.img
title old-kernel
        root (hd0,0)
        kernel /vmlinuz-2.4.9-21 ro root=/dev/hde8
        initrd /initrd-2.4.9-21.img
After the new kernel has proven to work, you may remove the lines for the old one from the GRUB config file, although it is best to wait a couple of days just to be sure.
Installing extra packages from the installation CDs

This is basically done in the same way as installing packages manually, except that you have to append the file system of the CD<i0/> to your machine's file system to make it accessible. On most systems, this will be done automatically upon insertion of a CD in the drive because the <c1>automount<i2/></c1> daemon is started up at boot time. If your CD is not made available automatically, issue the <c3>mount<i4/></c3> command in a terminal window. Depending on your actual system configuration, a line similar to this one will usually<i5/> do the trick:
On some systems, only <e0>root</e0> can mount removable media; this depends on the configuration.
For automation purposes, the CD drive usually has an entry in <f0>/etc/fstab<i1/></f0>, which lists the file systems and their mount points, that make up your file system tree. This is such a line:
This indicates that the system will understand the command <c0>mount <f1>/mnt/cdrom</f1></c0>. The <o2>noauto</o2> option means that on this system, CDs are not mounted at boot time.

You may even try to right click on the CD icon on your desktop to mount the CD if your file manager doesn't do it for you. You can check whether it worked issuing the <c0>mount<i1/></c0> command with no arguments:

After mounting the CD, you can change directories<i0/>, usually to the mount point <f1>/mnt/cdrom</f1>, where you can access the content of the CD-ROM. Use the same commands for dealing with files and directories as you would use for files on the hard disk.

In order to get the CD<i0/> out of the drive after you've finished using it, the file system on the CD should be unused. Even being in one of the subdirectories of the mount point, <f1>/mnt/cdrom</f1> in our example, will be considered as <q2>using the file system</q2>, so you should get out of there. Do this for instance by typing <c3>cd</c3> with no arguments, which will put you back in your home directory. After that, you can either use the command

<e0>NEVER</e0> force the drive. The trick with the paperclip is a bad idea, because this will eventually expunge the CD, but your system will think the CD is still there because normal procedures were not followed. Chances are likely that you will have to reboot to get the system back in a consistent state.

If you keep getting <q0>device busy</q0> messages, check first that all shell sessions have left the CD file system and that no graphical applications are using it anymore. When in doubt, use the <c1>lsof</c1> tool to trace down the process(es) still using the CD resource.
When everything has its place, that means already half the work is done.

While keeping order is important, it is equally important to feel at home in your environment, whether text or graphical. The text environment is controlled through the shell setup files. The graphical environment is primarily dependent on the X server configuration, on which a number of other applications are built, such as window and desktop managers and graphical applications, each with their own config files. You should read the system and program specific documentation to find out about how to configure them.
Regional settings such as keyboard setup, installing appropriate fonts and language support are best done at installation time.
Software is managed either automatically or manually using a package system.

In this chapter we will learn more about printers and printing files. After reading this part, you will be able to:
Preview documents before sending them to the printer
Choose a good printer that works with your Linux system
Print files and check on printer status
Find necessary documentation to install a printer
Getting the file to the printer
Printing from within an application is very easy, selecting the <m0><g1>Print</g1></m0> option from the menu.
From the command<i0/> line, use the <c1>lp<i2/></c1> or <c3>lpr<i4/></c3> command.
These commands can read from a pipe<i0/>, so you can print the output of commands using

There are many options available to tune the page layout, the number of copies, the printer that you want to print to if you have more than one available, paper size, one-side or double-sided printing if your printer supports this feature, margins and so on. Read the man pages for a complete overview.
Once the file is accepted in the print<i0/> queue, an identification number for the print job is assigned:
To view (query) the print queue, use the <c0>lpq<i1/></c0> or <c2>lpstat<i3/></c2> command. When entered without arguments, it displays the contents of the default print queue.

<p0>davy:~></p0> <c1>lpq</c1>
blob is ready and printing
Rank	Owner	Job	File(s)		Total Size
active	davy	253	profile		1024 bytes
<p2>davy:~></p2> <c3>lpstat</c3>
blob-253	davy	1024	Tue 25 Jul 2006 10:20_01 AM CEST
Which is the default printer<i0/> on a system that has access to multiple printers?
What is the status of my printer(s)?

<p0>davy:~></p0> <c1>lpstat <o2>-p</o2></c1>
printer blob now printing blob-253. enabled since Jan 01 18:01
Removing jobs from the print queue
If you don't like<i0/> what you see from the status commands, use <c1>lprm<i2/></c1> or <c3>cancel<i4/></c3> to delete jobs.
In the graphical environment, you may see a popup window telling you that the job has been canceled.
In larger environments, <c0>lpc</c0> may be used to control multiple printers. See the <a1>Info</a1> or man pages on each command.

There are many GUI print tools used as a front-end to <c0>lp</c0>, and most graphical applications have a print function that uses <c1>lp</c1>. See the built-in Help functions and program specific documentation for more.
Why are there two commands for every task related to printing?

Printing on UNIX and alikes has a long history. There used to be two rather different approaches: the BSD-style printing and the SystemV-style printing. For compatibility, Linux with CUPS supports the commands from both styles. Also note that <c0>lp</c0> does not behave exactly like <c1>lpr</c1>, <c2>lpq</c2> has somewhat different options than <c3>lpstat</c3> and <c4>lprm</c4> is almost, but not quite, like <c5>cancel</c5>. Which one you use is not important, just pick the commands that you are comfortable with, or that you may know from previous experiences with UNIX-like systems.

If we want to get something sensible out of the printer, files should be formatted first. Apart from an abundance of formatting software, Linux comes with the basic UNIX formatting tools and languages.
Modern Linux systems support direct printing, without any formatting by the user, of a range of file types: text, PDF, PostScript and several image formats like PNG, JPEG, BMP and GIF.

For those file formats that do need formatting, Linux comes with a lot of formatting<i0/> tools, such as the <c1>pdf2ps</c1>, <c2>fax2ps</c2> and <c3>a2ps</c3> commands, that convert other formats to PostScript. These commands can create files that can then be used on other systems that don't have all the conversion tools installed.

Apart from these command line tools there are a lot of graphical word processing programs. Several complete office suites are available, many are free. These do the formatting automatically upon submission of a print job. Just to name a few: <a0>OpenOffice.org</a0>, <a1>KOffice</a1>, <a2>AbiWord</a2>, <a3>WordPerfect</a3>, etc.
The following are common languages<i0/> in a printing context:

<c0>groff</c0>: GNU version<i1/> of the UNIX <c2>roff</c2> command. It is a front-end to the groff document formatting system. Normally it runs the <c3>troff</c3> command and a post-processor appropriate for the selected device. It allows generation of PostScript files.

<a0>TeX</a0> and the macro<i1/> package <a2>LaTeX</a2>: one of the most widely used markup languages on UNIX systems. Usually invoked as <c3>tex</c3>, it formats files and outputs a corresponding device-independent representation of the typeset document.

Technical works are <e0>still</e0> frequently written in <a1>LaTeX</a1> because of its support for mathematic formulas, although efforts are being made at <u2>W3C</u2> (the World Wide Web Consortium) to include this feature in other applications.

SGML<i0/> and XML<i1/>: Free parsers are available for UNIX and Linux. XML is the next generation SGML, it forms the basis for DocBook XML, a document system (this book is written in XML, for instance).

The man<i0/> pages contain pre-formatted <c1>troff<i2/></c1> data which has to be formatted before it can roll out of your printer. Printing<i3/> is done using the <o4>-t</o4> option to the <c5>man</c5> command:

Then print the PostScript file. If a default print destination is configured for your system/account, you can just issue the command <c0>man <o1>-t</o1> <p2>command</p2></c0> to send the formatted page to the printer directly.
Anything that you can send to the printer can normally be sent to the screen as well. Depending on the file format, you can use one of these commands<i0/>:
TeX dvi files: with <c0>xdvi<i1/></c0>, or with <a2>KDE</a2>'s <c3>kdvi<i4/></c3>.

PDF files: <c0>xpdf<i1/></c0>, <c2>kpdf<i3/></c2>, <c4>gpdf<i5/></c4> or Adobe's viewer, <c6>acroread<i7/></c6>, which is also available for free but is not free software. Adobe's reader supports PDF 1.6, the others only support PDF versions up to 1.5. The version of a PDF file can be determined using the <c8>file</c8> command.
From within applications, such as Firefox or OpenOffice, you can usually select <m0><g1>Print Preview</g1></m0> from one of the menus.

Until a couple of years ago, the choice for Linux users was simple: everyone ran the same old LPD from BSD's Net-2 code. Then <a0>LPRng</a0> became more popular, but nowadays most modern Linux distributions use <u1>CUPS</u1>, the Common UNIX Printing System<i2/>. <a3>CUPS<i4/></a3> is an implementation of the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP), an HTTP-like RFC standard replacement protocol for the venerable (and clunky) LPD protocol. CUPS is distributed under the GNU Public License. CUPS is also the default print system on MacOS X.

Most distributions come with a GUI for configuring networked and local (parallel port or USB) printers. They let you choose the printer type from a list and allow easy<i0/> testing. You don't have to bother about syntax and location of configuration files. Check your system documentation before you attempt installing your printer.
CUPS can also be configured using a web interface that runs on port 631 on your computer. To check if this feature is enabled, try browsing to <u0/> or <u1/>.

As more and more printer vendors make drivers for CUPS available, CUPS will allow easy connection with almost any printer<i0/> that you can plug into a serial, parallel, or USB port, plus any printer on the network. CUPS will ensure a uniform presentation to you and your applications of all different types of printers.
Printers that only come with a Win9x driver could be problematic if they have no other support. Check with <u0/> when in doubt.

In the past, your best choice would have been a printer with native PostScript support in the firmware, since nearly all UNIX or Linux software producing printable output, produces it in PostScript<i0/>, the publishing industry's printer control language of choice. PostScript printers are usually a bit more expensive, but it is a device-independent, open programming language and you're always 100% sure that they will work. These days, however, the importance of this rule of thumb is dwindling.

In this section, we will discuss what you can do as a user when something goes wrong. We won't discuss any problems that have to do with the daemon-part of the printing service, as that is a task for system administrators.

If you print the wrong file, the job may be canceled<i0/> using the command <c1>lprm <p2>jobID</p2></c1>, where jobID is in the form <e3>printername-printjobnumber</e3> (get it from information displayed by <c4>lpq</c4> or <c5>lpstat</c5>). This will work when other jobs are waiting to be printed in this printer's queue. However, you have to be really quick if you are the only one using this printer, since jobs are usually spooled and send to the printer in only seconds. Once they arrive on the printer, it is too late to remove jobs using Linux tools.

What you can try in those cases, or in cases where the wrong print driver is configured and only rubbish comes out of the printer, is power off the printer. However, that might not be the best course of action, as you might cause paper jams and other irregularities.
Use the <c0>lpq</c0> command and see if you can spot your job:

<p0>elly:~></p0> <c1>lpq</c1>
Printer: lp@blob
 Queue: 2 printable jobs
 Server: pid 29998 active
 Unspooler: pid 29999 active
 Status: waiting for subserver to exit at 09:43:20.699
 Rank   Owner/ID             Class Job Files          Size Time
1      elly@blob+997           A   997 (STDIN)         129 09:42:54
2      elly@blob+22            A    22 /etc/profile    917 09:43:20
Lots of printers have web interfaces these days, which can display status information by typing the printer's IP address in your web browser:

This GUI shows printer status using your browser. There is a trafic light indicating the status, and choices for managing the printer: view config, control panel, printer settings, online support and admin settings.
CUPS web interface versus printer web interface
Note that this is not the CUPS web interface and only works for printers supporting this feature. Check the documentation of your printer.

If your job ID is not there and not on the printer, contact your system administrator. If your job ID is listed in the output, check that the printer is currently printing. If so, just wait, your job will get done in due time.

If the printer is not printing, check that it has paper, check the physical connections to both electricity and data network. If that's okay, the printer may need restarting. Ask your system admin for advice.

In the case of a network printer, try printing from another host. If the printer is reachable from your own host (see <x0/> for the <c1>ping</c1> utility), you may try to put the formatted file on it, like <f2>file.ps</f2> in case of a PostScript printer, using an FTP client. If that works, your print system is misconfigured. If it doesn't work, maybe the printer doesn't understand the format you are feeding it.
The <u0>GNU/Linux Printing site</u0> contains more tips and tricks.
The Linux print service comes with a set of printing tools based on the standard UNIX LPD tools, whether it be the SystemV or BSD implementation. Below is a list of print-related commands.
Configuring and testing printers involves being in the possession of one, and having access to the <e0>root</e0> account. If so, you may try:
Installing the printer using the GUI on your system.
Printing a test page using the GUI.
Printing a test page using the <c0>lp</c0> command.
Print from within an application, for example Mozilla or OpenOffice, by choosing <m0><g1>File</g1><g2>Print</g2></m0> from the menu.
Disconnect the printer from the network or the local machine/print-server. What happens when you try to print something?
The following exercises can be done without printer or root access.
Try to make PostScript files from different source files, (e.g. HTML, PDF, man pages). Test the results with the <c0>gv</c0> viewer.
Check that the print daemon is running.
Print the files anyway. What happens?
Make a PostScript file using Mozilla. Test it with <c0>gv</c0>.
Convert it to PDF format. Test with <c0>xpdf</c0>.
How would you go about printing a GIF file from the command line?
Use <c0>a2ps</c0> to print the <f1>/etc/profile</f1> file to an output file. Test again with <c2>gv</c2>. What happens if you don't specify an output file?

Accidents will happen sooner or later. In this chapter, we'll discuss how to get data to a safe place using other hosts, floppy disks, CD-ROMs and tapes. We will also discuss the most popular compressing and archiving commands.
Upon completion of this chapter, you will know how to:
Make, query and unpack file archives
Handle floppy disks and make a boot disk for your system
Find documentation to use other backup devices and programs

Although Linux is one of the safest operating systems in existence, and even if it is designed to keep on going, data can get lost. Data loss is most often the consequence of user errors, but occasionally a system fault, such as a power or disk failure, is the cause, so it's always a good idea to keep an extra copy of sensitive and/or important data.

In most cases, we will first collect all the data to back up in a single archive file, which we will compress later on. The process of archiving<i0/> involves concatenating all listed files and taking out unnecessary blanks. In Linux, this is commonly done with the <c1>tar<i2/></c1> command. <c3>tar</c3> was originally designed to archive<i4/> data on tapes, but it can also make archives, known as <e5>tarballs<i6/></e5>.
<c0>tar</c0> has many options<i1/>, the most important ones are cited below:
<o0>-t</o0>: test, shows content of a tarball
<o0>-f</o0> <f1>archivedevice</f1>: use <f2>archivedevice</f2> as source/destination for the tarball, the device defaults to the first tape device (usually <f3>/dev/st0</f3> or something similar)
It is common to leave out the dash-prefix with <c0>tar</c0> options, as you can see from the examples below.

The archives<i0/> made with a proprietary <c1>tar</c1> version on one system, may be incompatible with <c2>tar</c2> on another proprietary system. This may cause much headaches, such as if the archive needs to be recovered on a system that doesn't exist anymore. Use the GNU <c3>tar</c3> version on all systems to prevent your system admin from bursting into tears. Linux always uses GNU tar. When working on other UNIX machines, enter <c4>tar <o5>--help</o5></c4> to find out which version you are using. Contact your system admin if you don't see the word GNU somewhere.
In the example below, an archive is created<i0/> and unpacked.

<p0>gaby:~></p0> <c1>ls images/</c1>
me+tux.jpg  nimf.jpg

<p2>gaby:~></p2> <c3>tar cvf images-in-a-dir.tar images/</c3>
images/
images/nimf.jpg
images/me+tux.jpg

<p4>gaby:~></p4> <c5>cd images</c5>

<p6>gaby:~/images></p6> <c7>tar cvf images-without-a-dir.tar *.jpg</c7>
me+tux.jpg
nimf.jpg

<p8>gaby:~/images></p8> <c9>cd</c9>

<p10>gaby:~></p10> <c11>ls */*.tar</c11>
images/images-without-a-dir.tar

<p12>gaby:~></p12> <c13>ls *.tar</c13>
images-in-a-dir.tar 

<p14>gaby:~></p14> <c15>tar xvf images-in-a-dir.tar </c15>
images/
images/nimf.jpg
images/me+tux.jpg

<p16>gaby:~></p16> <c17>tar tvf images/images-without-dir.tar </c17>
-rw-r--r-- gaby/gaby  42888 1999-06-30 20:52:25 me+tux.jpg
-rw-r--r-- gaby/gaby   7578 2000-01-26 12:58:46 nimf.jpg

<p18>gaby:~></p18> <c19>tar xvf images/images-without-a-dir.tar </c19>
me+tux.jpg
nimf.jpg

<p20>gaby:~></p20> <c21>ls *.jpg</c21>
me+tux.jpg  nimf.jpg

This example also illustrates the difference between a tarred directory and a bunch of tarred files. It is advisable to only compress directories, so files don't get spread all over when unpacking the tarball (which may be on another system, where you may not know which files were already there and which are the ones from the archive).
When a tape drive is connected to your machine and configured by your system administrator, the file names ending in <f0>.tar</f0> are replaced with the tape<i1/> device name, for example:
The directory <f0>mail</f0> and all the files it contains are compressed into a file that is written on the tape immediately. A content listing is displayed because we used the verbose option.

The <c0>tar</c0> tool supports the creation of incremental<i1/> backups, using the <o2>-N</o2> option. With this option, you can specify a date, and <c3>tar</c3> will check modification time of all specified files against this date. If files are changed more recent than date, they will be included in the backup. The example below uses the timestamp on a previous archive as the date value. First, the initial archive is created and the timestamp on the initial backup file is shown. Then a new file is created, upon which we take a new backup, containing only this new file:

<p0>jimmy:~></p0> <c1>tar cvpf /var/tmp/javaproggies.tar java/*.java</c1>
java/btw.java
java/error.java
java/hello.java
java/income2.java
java/income.java
java/inputdevice.java
java/input.java
java/master.java
java/method1.java
java/mood.java
java/moodywaitress.java
java/test3.java
java/TestOne.java
java/TestTwo.java
java/Vehicle.java

<p2>jimmy:~></p2> <c3>ls -l /var/tmp/javaproggies.tar</c3>
-rw-rw-r-- 1 jimmy   jimmy   10240 Jan 21 11:58 /var/tmp/javaproggies.tar

<p4>jimmy:~></p4> <c5>touch java/newprog.java</c5>

<p6>jimmy:~></p6> <c7>tar -N /var/tmp/javaproggies.tar \
-cvp /var/tmp/incremental1-javaproggies.tar java/*.java 2> /dev/null</c7>
java/newprog.java

<p8>jimmy:~></p8> <c9>cd /var/tmp/</c9>

<p10>jimmy:~></p10> <c11>tar xvf incremental1-javaproggies.tar</c11>
java/newprog.java
Standard errors are redirected to <f0>/dev/null</f0>. If you don't do this, <c1>tar</c1> will print a message for each unchanged file, telling you it won't be dumped.

This way of working has the disadvantage that it looks at timestamps on files. Say that you download an archive into the directory containing your backups, and the archive contains files that have been created two years ago. When checking the timestamps of those files against the timestamp on the initial archive, the new files will actually seem old to <c0>tar</c0>, and will not be included in an incremental backup made using the <o1>-N</o1> option.
A better choice would be the <o0>-g</o0> option, which will create a list of files to backup. When making incremental backups, files are checked against this list. This is how it works:

<p0>jimmy:~></p0> <c1>tar cvpf work-20030121.tar -g snapshot-20030121 work/</c1>
work/
work/file1
work/file2
work/file3

<p2>jimmy:~></p2> <c3>file snapshot-20030121</c3>
snapshot-20030121: ASCII text
The next day, user <e0>jimmy</e0> works on <f1>file3</f1> a bit more, and creates <f2>file4</f2>. At the end of the day, he makes a new backup:

<p0>jimmy:~></p0> <c1>tar cvpf work-20030122.tar -g snapshot-20030121 work/</c1>
work/
work/file3
work/file4

These are some very simple examples, but you could also use this kind of command in a cronjob (see <x0/>), which specifies for instance a snapshot file for the weekly backup and one for the daily backup. Snapshot files should be replaced when taking full backups, in that case.
More information can be found in the <c0>tar</c0> documentation.

As you could probably notice, <c0>tar</c0> is OK when we are talking about a simple directory, a set of files that belongs together. There are tools that are easier to manage, however, when you want to archive entire partitions or disks or larger projects. We just explain about <c1>tar</c1> here because it is a very popular tool for distributing archives. It will happen quite often that you need to install a software that comes in a so-called <q2>compressed tarball</q2>. See <x3/> for an easier way to perform regular backups.
Data, including tarballs, can be compressed<i0/> using zip tools. The <c1>gzip<i2/></c1> command will add the suffix .gz to the file name and remove the original file.

<p0>jimmy:~></p0> <c1>ls -la | grep tar</c1>
-rw-rw-r-- 1 jimmy  jimmy    61440 Jun  6 14:08 images-without-dir.tar

<p2>jimmy:~></p2> <c3>gzip images-without-dir.tar</c3> 

<p4>jimmy:~></p4> <c5>ls -la images-without-dir.tar.gz </c5>
-rw-rw-r-- 1 jimmy  jimmy    50562 Jun  6 14:08 images-without-dir.tar.gz
Uncompress gzipped files with the <o0>-d</o0> option<i1/>.
<c0>bzip2<i1/></c0> works in a similar way, but uses an improved compression algorithm, thus creating smaller files. See the <c2>bzip2</c2> info pages for more.

Linux software packages are often distributed in a gzipped tarball. The sensible thing to do after unpacking that kind of archives is find the <f0>README<i1/></f0> and read it. It will generally contain guidelines to installing the package.
The GNU <c0>tar</c0> command is aware of gzipped<i1/> files. Use the command
for unzipping and untarring <f0>.tar.gz</f0> or <f1>.tgz</f1> files. Use
for unpacking <c0>tar</c0> archives that were compressed with <c1>bzip2</c1>.

The GNU project provides us with the <c0>jar<i1/></c0> tool for creating Java archives. It is a Java application that combines multiple files into a single JAR<i2/> archive file. While also being a general purpose archiving and compression tool, based on ZIP and the ZLIB compression format, <c3>jar</c3> was mainly designed to facilitate the packing of Java code, applets and/or applications in a single file. When combined in a single archive, the components of a Java application, can be downloaded much faster.

Unlike <c0>tar</c0>, <c1>jar</c1> compresses by default, independent from other tools - because it is basically the Java version of <c2>zip</c2>. In addition, it allows individual entries in an archive to be signed by the author, so that origins can be authenticated.
The syntax is almost identical as for the <c0>tar</c0> command, we refer to <c1>info <p2>jar</p2></c1> for specific differences.

One noteworthy feature not really mentioned in the standard documentation is that <c0>jar</c0> will follow symbolic links. Data to which these links are pointing will be included in the archive. The default in <c1>tar</c1> is to only backup the symbolic link, but this behavior can be changed using the <o2>-h</o2> to <c3>tar</c3>.
Saving copies of your data on another host is a simple but accurate way of making backups. See <x0/> for more information on <c1>scp</c1>, <c2>ftp</c2> and more.
In the next section we'll discuss local backup devices.
Moving your data to a backup device
Making a copy on a floppy disk

On most Linux systems, users have access to the floppy disk<i0/> device. The name of the device may vary depending on the size and number of floppy drives, contact your system admin if you are unsure. On some systems, there will likely be a link <f1>/dev/floppy</f1> pointing to the right device, probably <f2>/dev/fd0</f2> (the auto-detecting floppy device) or <f3>/dev/fd0H1440</f3> (set for 1,44MB floppies).

<c0>fdformat<i1/></c0> is the low-level floppy disk formatting tool. It has the device name of the floppy disk as an option. <c2>fdformat</c2> will display an error when the floppy is write-protected.

<p0>emma:~></p0> <c1>fdformat /dev/fd0H1440</c1>
Double-sided, 80 tracks, 18 sec/track. Total capacity 1440 kB.
Formatting ... done
Verifying ... done
<p2>emma:~></p2>
The <c0>mformat<i1/></c0> command (from the mtools package) is used to create DOS-compatible floppies which can then be accessed using the <c2>mcopy</c2>, <c3>mdir</c3> and other m-commands.
This GUI allows for chosing the FS type and density.
After the floppy is formatted, it can be mounted into the file system and accessed as a normal, be it small, directory, usually via the <f0>/mnt/floppy</f0> entry.
Should you need it, install the <c0>mkbootdisk<i1/></c0> utility, which makes a floppy from which the current system can boot.
Using the <c0>dd</c0> command to dump data
The <c0>dd<i1/></c0> command can be used to put data on a disk, or get it off again, depending on the given input and output devices. An example<i2/>:

<p0>gaby:~></p0> <c1>dd if=images-without-dir.tar.gz of=/dev/fd0H1440</c1>
98+1 records in
98+1 records out

<p2>gaby~></p2> <c3>dd if=/dev/fd0H1440 of=/var/tmp/images.tar.gz</c3>
2880+0 records in
2880+0 records out

<p4>gaby:~></p4> <c5>ls /var/tmp/images*</c5>
/var/tmp/images.tar.gz

Note that the dumping is done on an unmounted device. Floppies created using this method will not be mountable in the file system, but it is of course the way to go for creating boot or rescue disks. For more information on the possibilities of <c0>dd</c0>, read the man pages.
This tool is part of the GNU <e0>coreutils</e0> package.
The <c0>dd</c0> command can also be used to make a raw dump of an entire hard disk.
Making a copy with a CD-writer

On some systems users are allowed to use the CD-writer<i0/> device. Your data will need to be formatted first. Use the <c1>mkisofs<i2/></c1> command to do this in the directory containing the files you want to backup. Check with <c3>df<i4/></c3> that enough disk space is available, because a new file<i5/> about the same size as the entire current directory will be created:

<p0>[rose@blob recordables]</p0> <c1>df -h .</c1>

<p2>[rose@blob recordables]</p2> <c3>du -h -s .</c3>
325M    .

<p4>[rose@blob recordables]</p4> <c5>mkisofs -J -r -o cd.iso .</c5>

<p0>[rose@blob recordables]</p0> <c1>cdrecord -dev 0,0,0 -speed=8 cd.iso</c1>

There are some graphical tools available to make it easier on you. One of the popular ones is <c0>xcdroast<i1/></c0>, which is freely available from <u2>the X-CD-Roast web site<i3/></u2> and is included on most systems and in the GNU directory. Both the KDE and Gnome desktop managers have facilities to make your own CDs.
Backups on/from jazz drives, USB devices and other removables
These devices are usually mounted into the file system. After the mount procedure, they are accessed as normal directories, so you can use the standard commands for manipulating files.
In the example below, images are copied from a USB<i0/> camera to the hard disk:

If the camera<i0/> is the only USB storage device that you ever connect to your system, this is safe. But keep in mind that USB devices are assigned entries in <f1>/dev</f1> as they are connected to the system. Thus, if you first connect a USB stick to your system, it will be on the <f2>/dev/sda</f2> entry, and if you connect your camera after that, it will be assigned to <f3>/dev/sdb</f3> - provided that you do not have any SCSI disks, which are also on <f4>/dev/sd*</f4>. On newer systems, since kernel 2.6, a hotplug system called HAL (Hardware Abstraction Layer) ensures that users don't have to deal with this burden. If you want to check where your device is, type <c5>dmesg<i6/></c5> after inserting<i7/> it.
You can now copy the files:
Likewise, a jazz drive may be mounted on <f0>/mnt/jazz</f0>.

Appropriate lines should be added in <f0>/etc/modules.conf<i1/></f0> and <f2>/etc/fstab<i3/></f2> to make this work. Refer to specific hardware HOWTOs for more information. On systems with a 2.6.x kernel or higher, you may also want to check the man pages for <c4>modprobe</c4> and <f5>modprobe.conf</f5>.
Backing up data using a tape device

This is done using <c0>tar</c0> (see above). The <c1>mt<i2/></c1> tool is used for controlling the magnetic tape<i3/> device, like <f4>/dev/st0</f4>. Entire books have been written about tape backup, therefore, refer to our reading-list in <x5/> for more information. Keep in mind that databases might need other backup procedures because of their architecture.

The appropriate backup commands are usually put in one of the <e0>cron</e0> directories in order to have them executed on a regular basis. In larger environments, the freely available <u1>Amanda</u1> backup suite or a commercial solution may be implemented to back up multiple machines. Working with tapes, however, is a system administration task beyond the scope of this document.
Most Linux distributions offer their own tools<i0/> for making your life easy. A short overview:
SuSE: <a0>YaST</a0> now includes expanded backup and restore modules.
RedHat: the <a0>File Roller</a0> tool provides visual management of (compressed) archives. They seem to be in favour of the X-CD-Roast tool for moving backups to an external device.

Most distributions come with the BSD <c0>dump<i1/></c0> and <c2>restore<i3/></c2> utilities for making backups of <e4>ext2</e4> and <e5>ext3</e5> file systems. This tool can write to a variety of devices and literally dumps the file(s) or file system bit per bit onto the specified device. Like <c6>dd</c6>, this allows for backing up special file types such as the ones in <f7>/dev</f7>.

The <c0>rsync<i1/></c0> program is a fast and flexible tool for remote backup<i2/>. It is common on UNIX and UNIX-like systems, easy to configure and use in scripts. While the <e3>r</e3> in <c4>rsync</c4> stands for <q5>remote</q5>, you do not need to take this all too literally. Your <q6>remote</q6> device might just as well be a USB storage device or another partition on your hard disk, you do not need to have two separated machines.
An example: rsync to a USB storage device
As discussed in <x0/>, we will first have to mount<i1/> the device. Possibly, this should be done as <e2>root</e2>:
More and more distributions give access to removable devices for non-prilileged users and mount USB devices, CD-ROMs and other removable devices automatically.

Note that this guideline requires USB support to be installed on your system. See <u0>the USB Guide</u0> for help if this does not work. Check with <c1>dmesg</c1> that <f2>/dev/sda1</f2> is indeed the device to mount.
Then you can start the actual backup, for instance of the <f0>/home/karl</f0> directory:

Encryption<i0/> is synonym to secrecy. In the context of backups, encryption can be very useful, for instance if you need to leave your backed up data in a place where you can not control access, such as the server of your provider.

Apart from that, encryption can be applied to E-mails as well: normally, mail is not encrypted and it is often sent in the open over the netwerk or the Internet. If your message contains sensitive information, better encrypt it.

On Linux systems you will find <a0>GnuPG</a0>, the <a1>GNU Privacy Guard<i2/></a1>, which is a suite of programs that are compatible with the PGP (<a3>Pretty Good Privacy</a3>) tools that are commercially available.

In this guide we will only discuss the very simple usage of the encryption tools and show what you will need in order to generate an encryption key and use it to encrypt data for yourself, which you can then safely store in a public place. More advanced usage directions can be found in the man pages of the various commands.

Before you can start encrypting your data, you need to create<i0/> a pair of keys. The pair consists of a private and a public key. You can send the public key to correspondents, who can use it to encrypt data for you, which you decrypt with your private key. You always keep the private key, never share it with somebody else, or they will be able to decrypt data that is only destined for you. Just to make sure that no accidents happen, the private key is protected with a password. The key pair is created using this command<i1/>:

Now the key pair is generated by a program that spawns random numbers and that is, among other factors, fed with the activity data of the system. So it is a good idea to start some programs now, to move the mouse cursor or to type some random characters in a terminal window. That way, the chances to generate a number that contains lots of different digits will be much bigger and the key will be more difficult to crack.

When your key has been created, you will get a message about the <e0>fingerprint<i1/></e0>. This is a sequence of 40 hexadecimal<i2/> numbers, which is so long that it is very, very hard to generate the same key twice, on any computer. You can be rather sure that this is a unique sequence. The short form of this key consists of your name, followed by the last 8 hexadecimal numbers.
